Industry observers note that muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

It has been revealed that we tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

In a recent development, once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning demonstrates up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

In a recent development, the language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:.

Industry observers note that this is a substantial model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI:.

Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.

The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses.

Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key.

Sources indicate that you can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section reveals how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

Industry observers note that first, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

Recent findings suggest that in the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

According to recent reports, now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

It has been revealed that the core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:.

It has been revealed that we trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

Sources indicate that we combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

It has been revealed that we initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

In a recent development, we tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes.

Hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:.

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

In a recent development, you can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Industry observers note that finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

Ares Capital Corporation is the administrative and collateral agent, Ares Capital Management LLC the lead arranger and bookrunner, and ACF Finco I LP the revolving agent.

According to recent reports, term loans bear interest at either the agreement’s Base Rate benchmark plus 4.50% or its Term SOFR benchmark plus 5.50%; revolving loans use Base Rate plus 2.75% or Term SOFR plus 3.75%. Term SOFR has a 1.00% floor, the Base Rate a 2.00% floor, and interest on the loans is payable solely in cash.

According to recent reports, both facilities mature on the fifth anniversary of the effective date. A springing provision can move maturity to 91 days before Tempus’s 0.75% convertible senior notes due 2030 unless those notes are repaid or converted first or specified liquidity requirements are met.

Sources indicate that certain Tempus subsidiaries will guarantee the obligations, which are secured by substantially all assets of Tempus and those subsidiaries. The agreement includes minimum-liquidity and minimum-revenue covenants. Revolving availability depends on eligible accounts receivable and certain qualified cash, subject to reserves and other limitations, and revolving interest can be charged on a minimum balance even when actual borrowings are lower.

It has been revealed that the cash election uses flexibility described in Tempus’s July 20, 2026 acquisition announcement. The merger agreement priced Personalis at $16.25 per common share, representing approximately $1.5 billion in enterprise value net of Tempus’s existing ownership. Consideration was originally structured as all stock, with Tempus holding an option to pay cash capped at 50% of the consideration and a floating exchange ratio capped at 0.3356 Tempus shares per Personalis share.

The cash estimate assumes 108,740,631 Personalis shares outstanding immediately before closing and no perfected appraisal demands. The number of shares designated for cash can automatically decrease, with a corresponding increase in the stock portion, to satisfy the merger agreement’s reorganization threshold, determined using Tempus’s closing-date trading price.

Tempus states the acquisition pairs its multimodal data, AI capabilities and commercial infrastructure with Personalis’s tumor-informed molecular residual disease (MRD) technology, including the NeXT Personal test, which detects small traces of circulating tumor DNA to monitor treatment response, residual cancer and recurrence.

Sources indicate that the transaction builds on a partnership established in November 2023, through which Tempus invested in Personalis and commercialized NeXT Personal. Tempus CEO Eric Lefkofsky called MRD “a large and rapidly growing market” and said the collaboration had demonstrated the strength of combining Personalis’s technology with his company’s commercial infrastructure.

Tempus originally expected the acquisition to close in late 2026 or early 2027. Closing remains subject to Personalis stockholder adoption of the merger agreement and other customary conditions. Tempus has now aligned the debt package with its cash-and-stock election, but the borrowing timetable and the proposed AI-supported MRD expansion both remain tied to completion of the acquisition.

Stale links on UK public sector websites direct visitors to gambling dens

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Consultancy finds 93 routes to casino promotions across 26 orgs, with defunct enterprise partnership domains repurposed.
  • UK public sector websites are directing visitors to gambling promotions through old links to defunct local enterprise partnerships (LEPs), research by digital consultancy Digital Royalty has found.
  • The consultancy identified 93 links across 79 pages on websites belonging to 26 public bodies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Consultancy finds 93 routes to casino promotions across 26 orgs, with defunct enterprise partnership domains repurposed.

UK public sector websites are directing visitors to gambling promotions through old links to defunct local enterprise partnerships (LEPs), research by digital consultancy Digital Royalty has found.

The consultancy identified 93 links across 79 pages on websites belonging to 26 public bodies.

LEPs brought together councils and businesses to promote economic growth in England under a coalition government initiative released in 2010. Central government funding ended in April 2024, with their core functions transferred to local and combined authorities.

According to recent reports, among other things, Digital Royalty builds and looks after websites, which means chasing down old links. In August, it found that a link on Surrey County Council's website led to a former LEP address now displaying casino content. It went looking for more.

Digital Royalty founder Alex De Sousa said: "Slow is usually a sign of caution and diligence, but 31 months after the LEPs wound up, it's crossed into inefficient and dangerous.".

Industry observers note that the consultancy offered The Register four examples of websites run by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), Hull City Council, Parliament, and the Local Government Association. One example is a government page about the Digital Skills Partnership, originally published under an earlier incarnation of DCMS.

The page includes a link that appears to be for the Humber Digital Skills Partnership within the Humber LEP website, but in fact takes users to a site advertising "Independent Non GamStop Casinos UK – New Casino Sites Outside GamStop." GamStop is the self-exclusion scheme designed to help people restrict their online gambling, which makes the links more concerning than ordinary website clutter.

The same link appears on the Hull City Council website under a list of Joint Committees, Partnerships and Trusts where it appears as Local Economic Partnership (Humber LEP).

An old page for the Parliament website detailing the Department for Business, Energy & Industrial Strategy committee's Industrial Strategy report includes a footnote (135) that appears to be for the Business Central funding finder service, but takes the user to the "Highest RTP Non GamStop Casinos for UK Players.".

Sources indicate that the Local Government Association's (LGA) sustainability and waste route map included a link to the former York and North Yorkshire LEP website. The destination initially appeared legitimate but contained links promoting crypto casinos. The LGA now appears to have removed the link.

All the organizations mentioned have been contacted by The Register to offer them the opportunity to comment.

Sources indicate that digital Royalty checked former web addresses associated with about 70 LEPs and growth hubs, then used a backlink index to identify roughly 3,000 incoming links from public sector sites. Most were simply outdated rather than leading to gambling content.

The findings are not exhaustive: the index may miss pages, and the research did not cover other types of defunct public body whose domains may have been repurposed. ®.

Breaking: Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use.
  • Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively.
  • It has been revealed that we introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

It has been revealed that we introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

It has been revealed that overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

Sources indicate that the multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the fresh release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

Recent findings suggest that we also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 indicates strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

Sources indicate that the results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

Sources indicate that the report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

In a recent development, access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been unveiled by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team unveiled the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In a recent development, in summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

Industry observers note that if you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Project Apertus, et al. “Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners.” arXiv:2610.15542. Preprint, arXiv, October 11, 2026. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.15542.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that fireworks AI made Tencent’s open-weight Hy4 Flash available on its serverless API on November 25, 2026, pricing the Standard tier at $0.07 per million input tokens and $0.281 per million output tokens. The announcement adds benchmark tests that position the model as a low-cost option for professional and agentic work.

Cached input costs $0.003 per million tokens. A Priority tier is also available, and the service is served globally. Developers can instead use on-demand dedicated GPUs; the Hy4 Flash model page lists function calling as supported and fine-tuning and embeddings as unsupported.

Industry observers note that hy4 Flash uses a mixture-of-experts design, in which only about 12 billion of its roughly 220 billion parameters are active for each token. It accepts text and image input. The native context window is 1M tokens, while Fireworks is serving 512K at launch, a material constraint for applications built around very long documents or extended agent sessions.

Tencent introduced Hy4 Flash on November 16, 2026, as its most cost-effective Hy model for everyday productivity and released the weights on GitHub, Hugging Face, ModelScope, and AtomGit. Tencent notes reinforcement learning reduced average end-to-end output tokens by 50%, while megakernels, 4-bit quantization, and DFly lifted decoding speed beyond 150 tokens per second.

Sources indicate that fireworks reports testing the model on seven professional benchmarks with the same harness used for other models on each leaderboard, at high reasoning. Costs are based on recorded tokens at Fireworks’ serverless prices, and the results are dated November 22, 2026. Hy4 Flash reached the score-cost Pareto frontier on every board where cost was recorded, meaning no listed model delivered a higher score at a lower cost.

Recent findings suggest that fireworks’ run of Epiq’s CorporateBench, which tests questions across thousands of internal company emails and meeting notes, produced a 75.9% score for Hy4 Flash: sixth of 14 models and slightly above Claude Opus 5.5’s 75.4%. The respective costs were $0.013 and $2.80 per task.

Tech giant was religious about backups but sinned by leaving them exposed

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (442 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Never put the backup server in the same Windows domain as production.
  • Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we’re thankful every time someone leaves a password sticky note on a monitor or fails to delete a terminated employee’s admin account.
  • Our story comes courtesy of Da Li, who serves as global alliance manager at Info2Soft, a company that provides data protection and recovery software.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Never put the backup server in the same Windows domain as production.

Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we’re thankful every time someone leaves a password sticky note on a monitor or fails to delete a terminated employee’s admin account. But neither of those common occurrences is what we’ll be talking about today. Instead, our subject broke the number-one rule of backups: you gotta keep ’em separated.

Our story comes courtesy of Da Li, who serves as global alliance manager at Info2Soft, a company that provides data protection and recovery software. At one point, a partner called him into a case where a Chinese vehicle parts manufacturer fell victim to a ransomware gang. Unfortunately, its backup was compromised too.

The manufacturer had religiously backed up its manufacturing execution system (MES) and SAP orders, inventory, and finance systems every night. There was even a green dashboard that indicated the backup process had succeeded, and someone checked that every morning.

However, one Friday evening, crims broke into the network and found out that the backup server was joined to the same Windows domain as the rest of the network. The hackers found a plaintext password for the backup service account in a maintenance script on a file share and discovered that someone had used the very same password for a domain admin account.

So the first thing the crooks did was delete every restore point on that backup server. Then they started encrypting the production servers to ransom them.

Sources indicate that “Every backup job had succeeded for three years,” Li said. “The failure was that the thing meant to save them could be reached with the same keys as the thing being attacked.”.

Have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com. Anonymity is available upon request.

The results were devastating. With the MES and SAP data both gone, the plant couldn't schedule production, ship parts, or track them.

By the time Li was called in, the plant had already resolved its ransomware situation. We don’t know whether it paid or not. The manufacturer did ask Li and his firm to make sure that this couldn’t happen again.

Recent findings suggest that li’s fix was not radical, but it was instructive. He made sure that the company now keeps its backup system outside the production domain, uses unique credentials, and requires MFA to reduce the risk of unauthorized access even if a password is compromised. He also made sure that the company keeps at least one offline backup and runs a test restore quarterly to ensure it’s prepared for emergencies.®.

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3322 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • It has been revealed that beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • Industry observers note that beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

It has been revealed that beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Industry observers note that beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post demonstrates you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

In a recent development, reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

It has been revealed that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

According to recent reports, beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

It has been revealed that the two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Recent findings suggest that attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

It has been revealed that the router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

In a recent development, the residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Recent findings suggest that every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Blueprint for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

It has been revealed that beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Sources indicate that pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

According to recent reports, beam's config defines an expert-parallel strategy. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

In a recent development, both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

Industry observers note that † Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

Industry observers note that you can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

According to recent reports, the quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

In a recent development, the setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

It has been revealed that training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Sources indicate that reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the fresh weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Industry observers note that upgrade: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Recent findings suggest that evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

According to recent reports, the next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

It has been revealed that at Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

In a recent development, we asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

Recent findings suggest that we used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

Industry observers note that you can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

It has been revealed that we wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

It has been revealed that our score-versus-latency plot indicates the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

It has been revealed that we wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

Recent findings suggest that first, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

This is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

In a recent development, one question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

In a recent development, S&P Global Ratings placed NVIDIA’s AA issuer credit rating and AA senior unsecured debt rating on CreditWatch with negative implications on November 25, 2026, citing concerns about board independence, executive oversight and succession planning. The agency said it could downgrade NVIDIA within 90 days if further due diligence finds that governance deficiencies remain.

The ratings were affirmed, with CreditWatch marking a review for a possible downgrade. The issuer rating moved from AA/Stable/A-1+ to AA/Watch Neg/A-1+, while the senior unsecured rating moved from AA to AA/Watch Neg. NVIDIA’s A-1+ commercial paper rating was affirmed separately.

In a recent development, the concerns center on the board’s structure, composition and effectiveness. S&P said events involving the CEO and questions about potential export-control violations exposed those weaknesses; the CEO’s departure and later reinstatement did not resolve its questions about oversight of the executive code of conduct. Weak executive oversight and a lack of succession planning also sharpened key-person concerns.

In S&P’s assessment, long director tenures may have compromised independence, while governance practices may have lagged NVIDIA’s rapid expansion and growing importance in global technology infrastructure. The agency revised the management-and-governance modifier used in its credit analysis to neutral from positive and was unaware of any remedial board action addressing the potential deficiencies.

Industry observers note that S&P intends to meet NVIDIA’s board and management to discuss board independence, effective management oversight and a credible leadership succession proposal. It expects any downgrade to be limited to one notch unless investigations or disclosures indicate harm to NVIDIA’s reputation or future business prospects.

In a recent development, export controls form a separate part of the assessment. NVIDIA’s China exposure raises questions about geopolitical risk management and internal controls, in S&P’s view. A conclusion that export-control rules were circumvented or violated, or that past disclosures about exposure to China and nearby regions were misleading or understated, would weigh on overall credit quality.

In a recent development, for now, S&P’s assessments of NVIDIA’s competitive position, technology leadership and financial profile remain unchanged. S&P said stricter export controls could reduce future growth prospects, while its published scores still classify business risk as strong, competitive position as excellent, financial risk as minimal and liquidity as exceptional, with an aa stand-alone credit profile.

The credit profile rests on a business S&P describes as data-center-scale AI infrastructure. Its platform covers chips, networking, systems and software for model training and inference, data analytics, scientific computing, robotics and 3D graphics. Compute and networking generated 90% of revenue in the fiscal year ended January 25, 2026, while graphics generated 10%. Its core end markets are data center, gaming, professional visualization and automotive.

According to recent reports, the review therefore separates NVIDIA’s operating and financial strength from the governance controls around it. S&P is testing whether board oversight and succession planning have kept pace with the company’s role in AI infrastructure; adverse export-control or disclosure findings could broaden the concern to its reputation and business prospects.

TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that torchNeuron provides a upcoming native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium.
  • TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a fresh backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.
  • 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that torchNeuron provides a upcoming native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a fresh backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

According to recent reports, to date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

Sources indicate that torchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Sources indicate that now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Sources indicate that here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:.

The command below rolls out training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Sources indicate that training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:.

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

Recent findings suggest that more and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

In a recent development, make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, customers can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

  • Peninsula Energy has temporarily shut down its Wyoming uranium operation after a "cybersecurity incident" affected plant and wellfield control systems.
  • The Australian uranium producer stated on Wednesday that it had activated its response procedures and brought in outside specialists following the attack on its US subsidiary, Strata Energy, which operates the Lance uranium project.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Peninsula Energy says plant and wellfield control systems were affected, with no restart date yet.

Peninsula Energy has temporarily shut down its Wyoming uranium operation after a "cybersecurity incident" affected plant and wellfield control systems.

The Australian uranium producer stated on Wednesday that it had activated its response procedures and brought in outside specialists following the attack on its US subsidiary, Strata Energy, which operates the Lance uranium project.

Peninsula Energy mentioned it believes the attack is "confined to the plant and wellfield operating and control systems," and that back-office functions, such as payroll and other corporate systems, in both the US and Australia, remain unaffected.

"The organization's immediate priorities have been to protect the safety of its employees, secure its operating systems, and work towards the restoration of operations in a safe and controlled manner," it noted in an enhancement to the Australian Securities Exchange.

The notification [PDF] went on to say that Peninsula Energy's investigations into the attack, including whether any data was compromised, remain ongoing.

According to recent reports, peninsula has not given a restart date and states it cannot yet assess the impact on its 2027 production guidance. Operations will remain suspended until recovery and safety checks are complete. "Peninsula will provide further updates to the market as material information becomes available," it said.

The disclosure of additional information came two days after Peninsula secured a short trading halt, which referenced a cybersecurity incident at its Wyoming site.

The November 23 filing [PDF] dated the incident to Friday evening in Western Australia. Wednesday's update clarified that Strata detected it on the morning of November 20, local US time.

Peninsula subsequently requested a voluntary suspension of trading until the earlier of November 30 or an announcement on restarting operations and any resulting change to production guidance.

Peninsula's Lance project is a uranium mining operation, extracting the element from underground deposits and turning it into uranium concentrate, aka yellowcake or U₃O₈.

Uranium concentrate is feedstock for nuclear fuel production, typically undergoing conversion, enrichment, and fabrication into uranium dioxide pellets before use in reactors.

The Lance central processing plant was constructed to produce a maximum of 2.0 million pounds (Mlb) of U₃O₈ annually, and is licensed for 3.0 Mlb.

Recent findings suggest that peninsula previously forecast production of 500,000 to 600,000 pounds in 2027, having withdrawn its 2026 guidance earlier this year following operational problems at Lance. It now says it will reassess the 2027 outlook once operations resume. ®.

  • If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • Recent findings suggest that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

Recent findings suggest that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the substantial matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

Recent findings suggest that MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

Sources indicate that A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In a recent development, in 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

Sources indicate that the decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

It has been revealed that working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

According to recent reports, audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:.

Recent findings suggest that token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Recent findings suggest that several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Sources indicate that work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

It has been revealed that once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

Industry observers note that scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

Sources indicate that the move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

In a recent development, bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

Sources indicate that pyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Rackspace is shutting down its low-cost Spot cloud service after a security breach, giving customers two weeks' notice to move their workloads and retrieve their data.
  • Sources indicate that in a notice posted on Tuesday, the cloud computing biz stated its Rackspace Spot service will cease operations at 1700 Central Time (2300 UTC) on December 8.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Customers face frantic scramble to migrate workloads and rotate compromised credentials.

Rackspace is shutting down its low-cost Spot cloud service after a security breach, giving customers two weeks' notice to move their workloads and retrieve their data.

Sources indicate that in a notice posted on Tuesday, the cloud computing biz stated its Rackspace Spot service will cease operations at 1700 Central Time (2300 UTC) on December 8. Any workloads still running at that point will be terminated, and customers will no longer be able to access their data.

"Following the recent security incident affecting Rackspace Spot, Rackspace has made the decision to wind down the service," the company stated. "Spot customers are being notified with the wind-down timeline, instructions for retrieving their data and steps to secure their environments.".

Customers will have to contend with the fallout from the breach while simultaneously trying to get their applications and data off the platform.

According to a customer notification seen by The Register, the attackers used leaked credentials to access parts of Rackspace Spot over a period of almost 22 hours on November 17. Rackspace only learned of the intrusion the following day, after a customer raised the alarm.

The intruders impersonated legitimate users, created pods in customer Kubernetes clusters, gained access to stored credentials known as Kubernetes Secrets, and listed nodes and storage volumes.

"With that access, they could have read any Secret in an affected user's clusters, and any Spot API token or refresh token that user held," Rackspace told customers.

Rackspace has since revoked the affected tokens and sessions, removed the pods planted by the intruders, and changed the affected platform and storage keys. Customers must also reissue API tokens, download new Kubernetes configuration files, and rotate credentials stored in their clusters, including database passwords and third-party API keys.

Sirish Raghuram, co-founder and chief growth officer of Platform9, which co-developed Spot with Rackspace, shed some light on the root cause in a November 20 GitHub post.

In a recent development, "An observability system was breached using a compromised credential," Raghuram wrote. "This was obviously a critical error on our part and we are very sorry we let this happen.".

Raghuram remarked the incident necessitated significant changes to the underlying infrastructure clusters, prolonging the outage.

Spot's selling point was cheap compute. The service operated an auction-based pricing model, allowing customers to bid for cloud infrastructure at a fraction of the cost of conventional on-demand instances. Rackspace advertised savings of up to 90 percent for customers willing to tolerate interruptions to their workloads. A permanent interruption probably wasn't what they had in mind.

According to recent reports, rackspace hasn't explained why it chose closure over recovery, revealed how many customers were affected, or said whether it will offer migration extensions. It did not respond to The Register's questions. ®.
